takeaways.q: Why do vague instructions like "be conservative" fail?
takeaways.a: They give no actionable decision boundary — the model can't calibrate what "conservative" means across contexts.

takeaways.q: Correct way to define code-review criteria in a prompt?
takeaways.a: Explicit categorical criteria: exactly what to flag (bugs, security vulnerabilities) and what to skip (style preferences, local patterns).

takeaways.q: How do high false positives in one category affect the system?
takeaways.a: They destroy developer trust in ALL categories, even accurate ones — trust bleeds across the whole output.

takeaways.q: What do you do with a high-false-positive category while iterating?
takeaways.a: Temporarily disable it while refining its prompt, restore trust, then re-enable the improved category.

takeaways.q: Why define severity levels with code examples rather than prose?
takeaways.a: Prose forces interpretation of subjective concepts; concrete code examples remove ambiguity and give consistent classification.

takeaways.q: Correct hierarchy for filtering findings?
takeaways.a: Explicit criteria first, confidence-based routing second. Never replace criteria with confidence thresholds.

takeaways.q: Why is LLM self-reported confidence poor for filtering?
takeaways.a: It's poorly calibrated — often confident about wrong findings and hesitant about right ones. Use it to route to review, not to replace criteria.

traps.trap: Choosing 'be conservative' or 'only report high-confidence findings' as valid prompt improvements
traps.why: Vague instructions don't improve precision. Specific categorical criteria for what to flag and skip are correct.

traps.trap: Assuming confidence thresholds fix false positive problems
traps.why: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated. Explicit criteria with code examples work better; confidence routing only after criteria exist.

traps.trap: Keeping all review categories active while iterating on high false-positive categories
traps.why: FPs in one category destroy trust in all. Temporarily disable problem categories while improving them.

takeaways.q: Most effective technique for consistent, well-formatted output?
takeaways.a: Few-shot examples — beats more instructions, confidence thresholds, or temperature tweaks.

takeaways.q: Three triggers that say "add few-shot examples"?
takeaways.a: Detailed instructions still give inconsistent formatting; inconsistent judgement on ambiguous cases; extraction returns empty fields for data that exists.

takeaways.q: How many few-shot examples?
takeaways.a: 2–4 targeted examples. Fewer than 2 doesn't set a pattern; more than 4 wastes tokens.

takeaways.q: What must each example include beyond input→output?
takeaways.a: Reasoning for why that action was chosen over alternatives — so the model generalises the judgement to novel cases.

takeaways.q: Side effect of few-shot examples on extraction?
takeaways.a: They reduce hallucination by showing how to handle structural variety without inventing data.

takeaways.q: How do examples reduce false positives in code review?
takeaways.a: Show both what to flag AND what to ignore, so the model separates real issues from benign patterns.

takeaways.q: When use tool_use + JSON schema instead of few-shot?
takeaways.a: For malformed JSON (syntax). Not for inconsistent formatting or judgement — those are few-shot problems.

traps.trap: Choosing 'add more detailed instructions' when output formatting is inconsistent
traps.why: If detailed instructions already exist and output is still inconsistent, more instructions won't help. Few-shot examples of the exact format will.

traps.trap: Thinking few-shot examples only teach literal pattern-matching
traps.why: With reasoning included, examples teach the decision principle and generalise to novel patterns.

traps.trap: Using confidence thresholds to fix inconsistent judgement calls
traps.why: Thresholds are poorly calibrated and miss the root cause. Examples showing correct judgement on ambiguous cases fix it directly.

takeaways.q: Most reliable way to get schema-compliant JSON?
takeaways.a: tool_use with a JSON schema — eliminates JSON syntax errors. Prompt-based JSON can be malformed.

takeaways.q: What does tool_choice control, and at what scope?
takeaways.a: Whether/how the model calls tools — per request, not per conversation. Modes: auto, any, forced specific tool.

takeaways.q: When use tool_choice "any" for extraction?
takeaways.a: Multiple extraction schemas and unknown document type — must call a tool, model picks which.

takeaways.q: When use forced tool_choice?
takeaways.a: To guarantee a mandatory first step (e.g., extract_metadata before enrichment). Max control, no flexibility.

takeaways.q: What does tool_use with a schema NOT prevent?
takeaways.a: Semantic errors: sums that don't match, values in the wrong field, fabricated data. Needs separate validation.

takeaways.q: How do you design fields to prevent fabrication?
takeaways.a: Make fields optional/nullable when the source may lack the info — allow honest nulls.

takeaways.q: Schema pattern for genuinely ambiguous cases?
takeaways.a: Add an "unclear" enum value so the model isn't forced to classify uncertain data.

takeaways.q: Schema pattern for extensible categories?
takeaways.a: An "other" enum value paired with a freeform detail string.

traps.trap: Believing tool_use with JSON schemas prevents all extraction errors
traps.why: It eliminates syntax errors only. Semantic errors — bad sums, wrong fields, fabricated values — need separate validation.

traps.trap: Confusing tool_choice 'auto' with 'any'
traps.why: 'auto' may return text (no guarantee). 'any' guarantees a tool call but the model chooses which. Unknown doc type + guaranteed structure → 'any'.

traps.trap: Making all schema fields required to ensure data completeness
traps.why: Required fields pressure the model to fabricate when info is absent. Optional/nullable allows honest nulls.

takeaways.q: What three things go back to the model on a retry?
takeaways.a: The original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error.

takeaways.q: Which errors do retries fix?
takeaways.a: Format mismatches, structural errors, misplaced values, maths errors — where the data exists in the source but was extracted wrongly.

takeaways.q: When should you NOT retry?
takeaways.a: When info is genuinely absent from the source or needs external knowledge. Flag for human review.

takeaways.q: How do you build self-correction into the schema?
takeaways.a: Extract both calculated_total and stated_total, plus a conflict_detected boolean to flag contradictions.

takeaways.q: Schema syntax errors vs semantic errors — what fixes each?
takeaways.a: Syntax (malformed JSON, wrong types) → tool_use. Semantic (wrong sums, misplaced values) → validation logic + retry loop.

takeaways.q: Role of Pydantic in validate-retry?
takeaways.a: Enforces cross-field business rules a JSON schema can't express, producing per-field error messages the retry feeds back.

takeaways.q: How do detected_pattern fields improve prompts?
takeaways.a: Track which patterns trigger findings and their dismissal rates; high-dismissal patterns show where to refine the prompt.

takeaways.q: Why is retry-with-error-feedback better than a naive retry?
takeaways.a: Without the specific error the model repeats its mistake; with it (e.g., 'items sum to £450, stated £500') it corrects precisely.

traps.trap: Assuming retries always work for extraction failures
traps.why: Retries can't produce info absent from the source. Distinguish fixable from unfixable.

traps.trap: Implementing retries without including the specific validation error
traps.why: Naive retries reproduce the same mistake. The model must see exactly what went wrong.

traps.trap: Relying on schema validation alone without semantic checks
traps.why: tool_use catches syntax. Wrong sums, misplaced values, fabrication need validation logic and retries.

traps.trap: Treating Pydantic as redundant once tool_use enforces a JSON schema
traps.why: Schemas can't express cross-field rules (matching sums, date ordering). Pydantic encodes them and gives per-field errors for retries.

takeaways.q: Message Batches API vs synchronous — when each?
takeaways.a: Batch for latency-tolerant work consumed later (overnight reports, weekly audits). Synchronous for blocking workflows where someone waits.

takeaways.q: Key constraints of the Message Batches API?
takeaways.a: 50% cost savings, up to 24h processing, no latency SLA, no multi-turn tool calling within a request, custom_id for correlation.

takeaways.q: How do you correlate batch requests with responses?
takeaways.a: Each request has a unique custom_id that appears on its result.

takeaways.q: Failure-handling pattern for batches?
takeaways.a: Identify failures by custom_id, resubmit only those with targeted changes (chunking, simpler prompt, examples). Refine prompts on a sample set first.

takeaways.q: How often to submit batches for a 30-hour SLA?
takeaways.a: SLA − 24h max window = 6h buffer. Submit every ~4 hours so a fresh batch is always in flight.

takeaways.q: Why refine the prompt on a sample before a big batch?
takeaways.a: 90% first-pass on 1,000 docs = 100 retries; 60% = 400 retries — 4× the resubmission cost.

takeaways.q: What happens if a batch exceeds 24 hours?
takeaways.a: It comes back expired — treat as failure and resubmit. Design for the worst case.

takeaways.q: Can the batch API do multi-turn tool calling?
takeaways.a: No. Workflows needing tool execution mid-request must use the synchronous API.

traps.trap: Switching all workflows to batch processing for cost savings
traps.why: Blocking workflows must stay synchronous — batch has no SLA and can take 24h.

traps.trap: Assuming batch results arrive quickly because they often do
traps.why: No latency SLA. Design around the 24-hour maximum, not best case.

traps.trap: Using batch API for workflows requiring multi-turn tool calling
traps.why: Not supported within a single request. Use the synchronous API.

takeaways.q: Why is same-session self-review weak?
takeaways.a: The model keeps its original reasoning chain and is less likely to question its decisions. An independent instance approaches it fresh.

takeaways.q: Three symptoms of attention dilution in single-pass multi-file reviews?
takeaways.a: Deep feedback on some files, superficial on others; obvious bugs missed mid-review; the same pattern flagged differently across files.

takeaways.q: How should large reviews be structured?
takeaways.a: Pass 1: per-file local analysis (focused attention). Pass 2: cross-file integration (data flow, contradictions, dependency conflicts).

takeaways.q: Why doesn't a bigger context window fix attention dilution?
takeaways.a: It's attention quality, not capacity — more text fits but attention is still uneven.

takeaways.q: Calibrated thresholds vs raw self-reported confidence?
takeaways.a: Raw confidence is uncalibrated. Calibrated thresholds are validated against labelled sets with known accuracy — usable for routing.

takeaways.q: Five-step production review architecture?
takeaways.a: Generation → per-file review (independent instances) → integration review → confidence routing of low-confidence findings to humans → calibration loop against labelled sets.

traps.trap: Choosing self-review in the same session as a viable review strategy
traps.why: The model retains generation reasoning. An independent instance catches far more subtle issues.

traps.trap: Using a single pass for large multi-file reviews
traps.why: Inconsistent depth, missed bugs, contradictory findings. Split into per-file passes plus an integration pass.

traps.trap: Switching to a larger context window model to fix attention dilution
traps.why: Bigger windows don't fix attention quality. Focused per-file passes do.

traps.trap: Using uncalibrated confidence scores for automated review routing
traps.why: Calibrate thresholds on labelled validation sets before routing on confidence.
